children: China’s rapid climb up the industrial value chain is creating a new competitive headache for Europe, with Germany among the countries most exposed as Chinese manufacturers increasingly challenge the machinery, automotive and capital-goods industries that have powered Europe’s largest economy.

A new analysis from the European Central Bank finds that China’s industrial transformation is producing sharply different effects across the European Union. Manufacturing-heavy economies face the greatest pressure as China expands high-tech production, pursues greater industrial self-sufficiency and competes more aggressively on price.

For investors, Germany stands out because the problem is coming from two directions. Chinese companies are increasingly competing with German manufacturers in global markets while China itself appears to need fewer European industrial imports.
China looks more like Germany

The ECB examined how closely the mix of goods exported by individual European countries resembles China's export portfolio. That overlap has increased since 2019, particularly among manufacturing economies such as Germany.

Much of the change comes from machinery and transportation equipment. China's automotive industry has expanded rapidly while its manufacturers have moved into more sophisticated, technology-intensive products. Those happen to be areas in which German companies have long enjoyed a formidable competitive position.
The implication isn't simply that Europe is importing more inexpensive Chinese goods. Chinese manufacturers increasingly make the same kinds of products European companies sell around the world.
That puts pressure on German automakers and industrial companies not only in China but also in third-party markets where price can play a larger role in purchasing decisions.
China needs less from Europe
The second problem may be even more consequential.

The ECB found that China's imports have become less aligned with the goods European countries export. The deterioration has been especially pronounced for Germany and Central European economies integrated into automotive and manufacturing supply chains.
Again, machinery and transportation equipment are central to the shift.

Several forces may be at work. Chinese manufacturers are replacing some imports with domestic production, other foreign suppliers are taking market share and weak Chinese domestic demand has reduced purchases.

Whatever the combination, the result is visible in trade flows. EU exports to China have declined markedly since 2019, with Germany suffering a particularly pronounced drop because of its concentration in manufacturing and capital goods.

For decades, China's industrialization created a lucrative market for German manufacturers selling cars, machine tools, chemicals and other sophisticated products. The ECB's analysis suggests the next stage of China's development looks considerably less comfortable for that business model.
Losing ground in global markets
Europe also faces increasing competition outside China.

The EU's share of global goods exports has declined even as world trade has continued expanding. The deterioration has been particularly noticeable in products and destinations where China has gained ground, including machinery and transportation equipment.

China's integration into Asian supply chains gives its companies another advantage there. In more price-sensitive markets, Chinese manufacturers may benefit from lower costs and broader product offerings.

There is one notable bright spot. European countries have increased their export market share in the United States while China's share has declined. The ECB said that may partly reflect trade shifting because of U.S.-China tensions. European gains have also been concentrated in higher-value products, suggesting the continent retains competitive advantages in some sophisticated industries.
Germany’s industrial model tested
The findings have particular relevance for investors with exposure to German automakers, industrial-equipment makers and their suppliers.

China isn't simply another low-cost manufacturing competitor anymore. Its companies have increasingly moved into industries that sit near the heart of Germany's export economy. At the same time, China's push for industrial self-reliance potentially reduces a market that German companies once counted on for growth.

There is another vulnerability. Some European economies facing the greatest Chinese competition also have substantial exposure to industries dependent on critical raw materials. That creates potential supply-chain risks if China restricts exports of strategically important materials.

The ECB stops well short of declaring Europe's industrial model doomed. Lower-cost Chinese imports can benefit European companies and consumers, while investment and technology spillovers may create opportunities. European manufacturers also continue to demonstrate competitive strength in higher-value segments.

But the report points toward a structural shift investors may need to consider when valuing German industrial companies. China was once primarily a huge new customer for German manufacturing expertise. Increasingly, it is also a supplier, technological rival and global export competitor.

That leaves Germany unusually exposed to what might be called China's industrial graduation: the world's biggest manufacturing economy is moving deeper into precisely the businesses that Germany has traditionally done best.
